claim: Varenicline reduced nicotine upregulation of α4β2-type nicotinic receptors in live cells and neurons.
source: Varenicline reduced nicotine upregulation of α4β2-type nicotinic receptors (α4β2Rs) in live cells and neurons, but not for membrane preparations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 125I-epibatidine binding assays and patch-clamp recordings shown in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: Varenicline did not reduce nicotine upregulation of α4β2Rs in membrane preparations.
source: Varenicline reduced nicotine upregulation of α4β2-type nicotinic receptors (α4β2Rs) in live cells and neurons, but not for membrane preparations.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 125I-epibatidine binding assays on membrane preparations shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Effects of varenicline on upregulation depended on intracellular pH homeostasis.
source: Effects on upregulation depended on intracellular pH homeostasis and were not observed if acidic pH in intracellular compartments was neutralized.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that NH4Cl treatment, which neutralizes acidic compartments, eliminated varenicline's effects on upregulation (Figure 1D).

claim: Varenicline was trapped as a weak base in acidic compartments and slowly released.
source: Varenicline was trapped as a weak base in acidic compartments and slowly released, blocking 125I-epibatidine binding and desensitizing α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects in live cells versus membrane preparations, and reversal with pH neutralization (Figures 1, 2).

claim: Trapped varenicline blocked 125I-epibatidine binding.
source: Varenicline was trapped as a weak base in acidic compartments and slowly released, blocking 125I-epibatidine binding and desensitizing α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from 125I-epibatidine binding assays showing reduced binding in varenicline-treated cells (Figure 1B).

claim: Trapped varenicline desensitized α4β2Rs.
source: Varenicline was trapped as a weak base in acidic compartments and slowly released, blocking 125I-epibatidine binding and desensitizing α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from patch-clamp recordings showing reduced ACh-evoked currents (Figure 2).

claim: Epibatidine itself was trapped in acidic vesicles.
source: Epibatidine itself was trapped; 125I-epibatidine slow release from acidic vesicles was directly measured and required the presence of α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing biphasic dissociation kinetics of 125I-epibatidine from live cells (Figure 4A).

claim: 125I-epibatidine slow release from acidic vesicles was directly measured.
source: Epibatidine itself was trapped; 125I-epibatidine slow release from acidic vesicles was directly measured and required the presence of α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing slow dissociation component with rate constant of 6.0 × 10−6 sec−1 (Figure 4A).

claim: 125I-epibatidine trapping required the presence of α4β2Rs.
source: Epibatidine itself was trapped; 125I-epibatidine slow release from acidic vesicles was directly measured and required the presence of α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing that HEK cells lacking α4β2Rs had only ~1% of the 125I-epibatidine binding observed in α4β2R-expressing cells (Figure 4D).

claim: Nicotine exposure increased epibatidine trapping by increasing the numbers of acidic vesicles containing α4β2Rs.
source: Nicotine exposure increased epibatidine trapping by increasing the numbers of acidic vesicles containing α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing 4-5-fold increase in trapped 125I-epibatidine with nicotine treatment (Figure 4F) and increased numbers of α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles visualized with pHluorin-tagged α4 subunits (Figure 5).

claim: Tobacco is the leading cause of preventable deaths in the United States.
source: Tobacco continues to be widely used world-wide, primarily via cigarette smoking, and is the leading cause of preventable deaths in the United States (National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion (US) Office on Smoking and Health, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to National Center for Chronic Disease Prevention and Health Promotion report.

claim: Currently approved treatments for smoking cessation are nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, and varenicline.
source: The currently approved treatments for smoking cessation are nicotine replacement therapy, bupropion, and varenicline (Chantix).
evidence: Supported by established clinical knowledge about approved smoking cessation treatments.

claim: Varenicline is the most effective smoking cessation treatment.
source: While varenicline is the most effective, successful quit rates only reach ~50% of smokers (Agboola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agboola et al., 2015.

claim: Successful quit rates with varenicline only reach ~50% of smokers.
source: While varenicline is the most effective, successful quit rates only reach ~50% of smokers (Agboola et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Agboola et al., 2015.

claim: Nicotine binds to high-affinity nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in the brain.
source: Nicotine binds to high-affinity nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the brain, and binding initiates its addictive effects.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about nicotine's mechanism of action.

claim: Nicotine binding to nAChRs initiates its addictive effects.
source: Nicotine binds to high-affinity nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) in the brain, and binding initiates its addictive effects.
evidence: Supported by established scientific knowledge about nicotine addiction.

claim: nAChRs are members of the Cys-loop family of ligand-gated ion channels.
source: nAChRs are members of the Cys-loop family of ligand-gated ion channels, all of which are pentameric neurotransmitter receptors (Karlin, 2002; Albuquerque et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karlin, 2002 and Albuquerque et al., 2009.

claim: nAChRs are pentameric neurotransmitter receptors.
source: nAChRs are members of the Cys-loop family of ligand-gated ion channels, all of which are pentameric neurotransmitter receptors (Karlin, 2002; Albuquerque et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karlin, 2002 and Albuquerque et al., 2009.

claim: In the mammalian CNS, critical nicotine binding sites are nAChRs composed of α2-α6 and β2-β4 subunits.
source: In the mammalian CNS, these critical binding sites are nAChRs composed of α2 - α6 and β2 - β4 subunits; the most predominant contains α4 and β2 subunits (Lindstrom, 1996; McGehee and Role, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindstrom, 1996 and McGehee and Role, 1995.

claim: The most predominant nAChR in the mammalian CNS contains α4 and β2 subunits.
source: In the mammalian CNS, these critical binding sites are nAChRs composed of α2 - α6 and β2 - β4 subunits; the most predominant contains α4 and β2 subunits (Lindstrom, 1996; McGehee and Role, 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lindstrom, 1996 and McGehee and Role, 1995.

claim: The α4β2 nAChR subtype is closely linked to nicotine addiction.
source: The α4β2 nAChR subtype (α4β2R) is closely linked to nicotine addiction (Govind et al., 2009; Vezina et al., 2007; Lewis and Picciotto, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Govind et al., 2009; Vezina et al., 2007; and Lewis and Picciotto, 2013.

claim: Loss of either α4 or β2 subunit in knockout mice reduces the pharmacological and behavioral effects of nicotine.
source: Loss of either subunit in α4 or β2 subunit knockout mice reduces the pharmacological and behavioral effects of nicotine (Picciotto et al., 1998; Marubio et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Picciotto et al., 1998 and Marubio et al., 2003.

claim: Targeted expression of β2 subunits in the VTA of β2-knockout mice rescues nicotine-seeking behavior and nicotine-induced dopamine release.
source: In addition, targeted expression of β2 subunits in the brain ventral tegmental area (VTA) of β2-knockout mice rescues nicotine-seeking behavior and nicotine-induced dopamine release (Maskos et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maskos et al., 2005.

claim: Varenicline is a high-affinity partial agonist for α4β2R.
source: Varenicline is a high-affinity partial agonist for α4β2R.
evidence: Supported by established pharmacological knowledge about varenicline.

claim: Varenicline was designed as a smoking cessation reagent based on the idea that a partial agonist could compete for and reduce cell-surface α4β2R activation by nicotine.
source: The rationale for its design as a smoking cessation reagent was predicated on the idea that a partial agonist could compete for and reduce cell-surface α4β2R activation by nicotine, reduce dopamine overflow in the mesolimbic reward system and thereby reduce the reward sensation of smoking (Rollema et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2007.

claim: Varenicline reduces the rapid effects of nicotine on α4β2Rs in VTA dopaminergic neurons.
source: Varenicline does indeed reduce the rapid effects of nicotine on α4β2Rs in VTA dopaminergic neurons and acutely reduces nicotine-induced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens (Rollema et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2007.

claim: Varenicline acutely reduces nicotine-induced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens.
source: Varenicline does indeed reduce the rapid effects of nicotine on α4β2Rs in VTA dopaminergic neurons and acutely reduces nicotine-induced dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens (Rollema et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2007.

claim: Nicotine upregulation of nAChRs is linked to different processes in nicotine addiction, including sensitization and withdrawal.
source: Nicotine upregulation of nAChRs is linked to different processes in nicotine addiction, including sensitization (Govind et al., 2009; Vezina et al., 2007) and withdrawal (De Biasi et al., 2011) and is the only effect of nicotine on nAChRs that lasts longer than a few minutes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Govind et al., 2009; Vezina et al., 2007; and De Biasi et al., 2011.

claim: Nicotine upregulation is the only effect of nicotine on nAChRs that lasts longer than a few minutes.
source: Nicotine upregulation of nAChRs is linked to different processes in nicotine addiction, including sensitization (Govind et al., 2009; Vezina et al., 2007) and withdrawal (De Biasi et al., 2011) and is the only effect of nicotine on nAChRs that lasts longer than a few minutes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Govind et al., 2009; Vezina et al., 2007; and De Biasi et al., 2011.

claim: Upregulation occurs when nicotine exposure increases high-affinity nicotine-binding sites in brain.
source: Upregulation occurs when nicotine exposure increases high-affinity nicotine-binding sites in brain, measured by radiolabeled agonists such as nicotine (Marks et al., 1983; Schwartz and Kellar, 1983; Benwell et al., 1988; Breese et al., 1997) or epibatidine (Perry et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marks et al., 1983; Schwartz and Kellar, 1983; Benwell et al., 1988; Breese et al., 1997; and Perry et al., 1999.

claim: Chronic varenicline exposure in mice induces upregulation to the same degree, or even more than, chronic nicotine exposure when measured using 3H-epibatidine binding to membrane preparations.
source: Chronic varenicline exposure in mice induces upregulation to the same degree, or even more than, chronic nicotine exposure when measured using 3H-epibatidine binding to membrane preparations from different brain regions (Hussmann et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hussmann et al., 2012 and Turner et al., 2011.

claim: Reversal of α4β2R upregulation was correlated with less smoking relapse in humans.
source: Recent studies using PET imaging in humans found that reversal of α4β2R upregulation was correlated with less smoking relapse (Brody et al., 2013; Staley et al., 2006; Cosgrove et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brody et al., 2013; Staley et al., 2006; and Cosgrove et al., 2009.

claim: Varenicline at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells following 17 hr of exposure.
source: Varenicline (Figure 1A) at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Figure 1B, 'Var', red columns in the left, 'live cells' half of the graph) nor in cortical neurons (Figure 1F, left) following 17 hr of exposure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1F.

claim: Varenicline at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in cortical neurons following 17 hr of exposure.
source: Varenicline (Figure 1A) at 30 μM did not upregulate 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Figure 1B, 'Var', red columns in the left, 'live cells' half of the graph) nor in cortical neurons (Figure 1F, left) following 17 hr of exposure.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: A full concentration-response curve with chronic varenicline revealed an inverted U-shaped dependence of upregulation of binding that peaked at 60–70% of that observed with nicotine at varenicline concentrations between 100 nM and 1 μM.
source: However, a full concentration-response curve with chronic varenicline revealed an inverted U-shaped dependence of upregulation of binding that peaked at 60–70% of that observed with nicotine, which occurred at varenicline concentrations between 100 nM and 1 μM (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, black circles).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Varenicline (30 μM) co-applied with nicotine prevented nicotine upregulation of binding in both heterologous cells and cortical neurons.
source: When co-applied with nicotine, varenicline (30 μM) prevented nicotine upregulation of binding in both heterologous cells and cortical neurons (Figure 1B,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1F.

claim: The reversal of the actions of nicotine on α4β2R binding by varenicline was concentration-dependent, with upregulation decreasing exponentially with increased varenicline concentration.
source: The reversal of the actions of nicotine on α4β2R binding also was concentration-dependent, with upregulation decreasing exponentially with increased varenicline concentration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, black squares).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Varenicline concentrations in the brain are likely to be higher than in plasma because of the presence of high-affinity binding to nAChRs.
source: Recent studies indicate that varenicline concentrations in the brain are likely to be higher than in plasma because of the presence of high-affinity binding to nAChRs (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010.

claim: Unbound varenicline concentrations in the brain fall in the range of 32 to 131 nM.
source: Based on this study's estimates, unbound varenicline concentrations in the brain fall in the range of 32 to 131 nM and plasma concentrations are approximately 4-fold lower.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010 study.

claim: Varenicline plasma concentrations are approximately 4-fold lower than brain concentrations.
source: Based on this study's estimates, unbound varenicline concentrations in the brain fall in the range of 32 to 131 nM and plasma concentrations are approximately 4-fold lower.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010 study.

claim: A previous study found differences in varenicline binding to human α4β2Rs compared to rat α4β2Rs when expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
source: In addition, a previous study found differences in varencilcine binding to human α4β2Rs compared to rat α4β2Rs when expressed in Xenopus oocytes (Papke et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Papke et al., 2010.

claim: At 100 nM varenicline, nicotine upregulation was significantly reduced to ~60% of the level without varenicline for both rat and human α4β2Rs.
source: We found that at 100 nM varenicline nicotine upregulation was significantly reduced to ~60% of the level without varencline (Figure 1G) for both rat and human α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There were no significant differences between rat and human α4β2Rs at 0, 100 nM and 30 μM varenicline.
source: We also found no significant differences between rat and human α4β2Rs at 0, 100 nM and 30 μM varenicline (Figure 1G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Varenicline should reduce nicotine upregulation at concentrations expected to exist in brain.
source: These results indicate that varenicline should reduce nicotine upregulation at concentrations expected to exist in brain.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing effects at 100 nM and estimates of brain concentrations.

claim: Varenicline is unlikely to act as a partial agonist at concentrations expected in brain.
source: In contrast, varenicline is unlikely to act as a partial agonist at these concentrations (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollema et al., 2010.

claim: Lobeline has smoking cessation activity.
source: Another nAChR partial agonist, lobeline, reported to have smoking cessation activity (Damaj et al., 1997; Miller et al., 2003) had effects similar to those of varenicline (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Damaj et al., 1997 and Miller et al., 2003.

claim: Chronic exposure to lobeline alone or together with nicotine reduced 125I-epibatidine binding levels below that observed for the untreated cells and neurons.
source: Chronic exposure to lobeline alone or together with nicotine reduced 125I-epibatidine binding levels below that observed for the untreated cells and neurons ('Lob', blue columns in the left, 'live cells' half of the graphs in Figure 1B,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1F.

claim: The inverted U-shaped concentration-dependence of lobeline effects on upregulation was similar to that of varenicline, with 125I-epibatidine binding peaking at ~50% of nicotine-induced upregulation at 100 nM – 1 μM.
source: The inverted U-shaped concentration-dependence of lobeline effects on upregulation was similar to that of varenicline. 125I-epibatidine binding peaked at ~50% of nicotine-induced upregulation, was maximal at 100 nM – 1 μM, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C, black circles), and co-incubation with nicotine reduced upregulation exponentially with increasing concentrations of lobeline (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D, black squares).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and 1D.

claim: If 125I-epibatidine binding was performed on membrane fragments instead of intact cells, varenicline upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells to the same degree as nicotine and did not reduce nicotine upregulation.
source: If 125I-epibatidine binding was performed on membrane fragments instead of intact cells, varenicline upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells to the same degree as nicotine and did not reduce nicotine upregulation (Figure 1B, red columns on right, 'membranes' half of the graph).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lobeline exposure upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to about 50% of that observed with nicotine treatment in membrane fragments.
source: Lobeline exposure upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to about 50% of that of observed with nicotine treatment and reduced nicotine upregulation by 50% (Figure 1B, blue columns on right half of the graph).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Lobeline reduced nicotine upregulation by 50% in membrane fragments.
source: Lobeline exposure upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to about 50% of that of observed with nicotine treatment and reduced nicotine upregulation by 50% (Figure 1B, blue columns on right half of the graph).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Previous studies found that chronic varenicline exposure upregulated 3H-epibatidine binding to brain tissue to the same degree as nicotine and reported no effect of varenicline exposure on nicotine upregulation.
source: The effects of varenicline and lobeline on nicotine upregulation were therefore distinct in live cells and membrane fragments, which could explain why previous studies found that chronic varenicline exposure upregulated 3H-epibatidine binding to brain tissue to the same degree as nicotine and reported no effect of varenicline exposure on nicotine upregulation (Hussmann et al., 2012; Turner et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hussmann et al., 2012 and Turner et al., 2011.

claim: Previous studies on varenicline upregulation were done with membrane preparations.
source: These experiments were done with membrane preparations, whereas the suppressive activity of varenicline on nicotine upregulation was only observed in intact cells.
evidence: Inferred from citations to Hussmann et al., 2012 and Turner et al., 2011.

claim: Nicotine was described previously as being concentrated and trapped in intracellular acidic compartments in Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs.
source: This process was described previously for nicotine in Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs (Jia et al., 2003); furthermore, slow release of nicotine from acidic compartments caused α4β2R desensitization, thereby reducing ACh-induced α4β2R currents.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003.

claim: Slow release of nicotine from acidic compartments caused α4β2R desensitization in Xenopus oocytes.
source: This process was described previously for nicotine in Xenopus oocytes expressing α4β2Rs (Jia et al., 2003); furthermore, slow release of nicotine from acidic compartments caused α4β2R desensitization, thereby reducing ACh-induced α4β2R currents.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003.

claim: NH4Cl treatment altered the effects of varenicline and lobeline on 125I-epibatidine binding such that both ligands produced upregulation of binding.
source: NH4Cl treatment altered the effects of varenicline and lobeline on 125I-epibatidine binding; both ligands produced upregulation of binding (Figure 1D left half, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C), in contrast to their actions at physiological pH (Figure 1B, leftmost trio of columns).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,C.

claim: NH4Cl exposure following co-incubation with nicotine relieved the suppression of upregulation by varenicline and lobeline.
source: Moreover, NH4Cl exposure following co-incubation with nicotine relieved the suppression of upregulation by varenicline and lobeline (Figure 1D, right trio of columns, Figure 1-figure supplement B, D), such that 125I-epibatidine binding in these conditions were indeed similar to the results using membrane preparations (Figure 1B, rightmost trio of columns).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,D.

claim: NH4Cl treatment of cultured cortical neurons had similar effects on 125I-epibatidine binding after varenicline or lobeline exposures as in HEK cells.
source: NH4Cl treatment of cultured cortical neurons had similar effects on 125I-epibatidine binding after varenicline or lobeline exposures (Figure 1F, right half of graph).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Incubation with the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A (50 nM) produced similar 125I-epibatidine binding results as NH4Cl treatment.
source: We also obtained similar 125I-epibatidine binding results with HEK cells using two other methods to reduce the pH gradient - incubation with the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A (Baf, 50 nM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or with the weak base chloroquine (Chlor, 150 μM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Incubation with the weak base chloroquine (150 μM) produced similar 125I-epibatidine binding results as NH4Cl treatment.
source: We also obtained similar 125I-epibatidine binding results with HEK cells using two other methods to reduce the pH gradient - incubation with the proton pump inhibitor bafilomycin A (Baf, 50 nM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A) or with the weak base chloroquine (Chlor, 150 μM; Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Nicotine upregulation of currents from α4β2R-expressing HEK cells was observed as an increase by ~5 fold in mean peak current amplitudes.
source: Nicotine upregulation of currents from α4β2R-expressing HEK cells was observed as an increase by ~5 fold in mean peak current amplitudes (e.g., Figure 2A, white vs. black column).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Varenicline exposure alone did not alter nAChR current amplitudes.
source: Exposure to varenicline alone did not alter nAChR current amplitudes, whereas lobeline reduced the mean amplitude to below that of control (untreated) receptor currents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Lobeline exposure reduced the mean nAChR current amplitude to below that of control (untreated) receptor currents.
source: Exposure to varenicline alone did not alter nAChR current amplitudes, whereas lobeline reduced the mean amplitude to below that of control (untreated) receptor currents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: When co-incubated with nicotine, both varenicline and lobeline occluded functional upregulation.
source: When co-incubated with nicotine, both varenicline and lobeline occluded functional upregulation; lobeline treatment again reduced nAChR currents to a mean amplitude below even that of the control group.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Neither varenicline nor lobeline treatment changed the time course of desensitization of the ACh currents.
source: Neither treatment changed the time course of desensitization of the ACh currents.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: NH4Cl (20 mM) treatment partly restored nicotine-induced functional upregulation of ACh currents in lobeline and varenicline treated α4β2R-expressing HEK cells.
source: NH4Cl (20 mM) treatment also partly restored nicotine-induced functional upregulation of ACh currents in lobeline and varenicline treated α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Figure 2C,D), albeit to a lesser degree than as observed with the binding experiments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: 125I-epibatidine binding was highly reduced for cells that received the bathing solution from cells chronically treated with varenicline or lobeline as compared to untreated cells.
source: Consistent with the release of varenicline and lobeline from intracellular acidic compartments, 125I-epibatidine binding was highly reduced for cells that received the bathing solution from cells chronically treated with varenicline or lobeline as compared to untreated cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Nicotine upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding from live cells was similar to that in membrane preparations.
source: Nicotine upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding from live cells was similar to that in membrane preparations (Figure 1) and following neutralization of the pH gradient of acidic compartments (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1 and Figure 1D.

claim: Functional upregulation of ACh currents by nicotine did not change if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished.
source: Functional upregulation of ACh currents by nicotine also did not change if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Nicotine is not trapped in the acidic compartment of α4β2R-expressing HEK cells.
source: These observations are consistent with previous findings that nicotine is not trapped in the acidic compartment of α4β2R-expressing HEK cells (Jia et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jia et al., 2003 and experimental data in Figures 1 and 2.

claim: DHβE is a weak base and a α4β2R competitive antagonist.
source: Dihydro-beta-erythroid (DHβE, Figure 3A) is a weak base and a α4β2R competitive antagonist.
evidence: Supported by established pharmacological knowledge about DHβE.

claim: DHβE was found to induce upregulation of α4β2R high-affinity binding sites.
source: Despite being a competitive antagonist, DHβE was found to induce upregulation of α4β2R high-affinity binding sites (Whiteaker et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Whiteaker et al., 1998.

claim: A 2-fold upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding was observed with 17 hr of exposure of the cells to 100 μM DHβE.
source: Consistent with previous findings, we observed a 2-fold upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding with 17 hr of exposure of the cells to 100 μM DHβE (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Acute application of DHβE at 100 μM completely inhibits ACh-induced currents.
source: At this concentration, acute application of DHβE completely inhibits ACh-induced currents (data not shown), as was shown previously (Wu et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2006.

claim: Prolonged DHβE exposure upregulated ACh-induced currents, similar to the binding sites.
source: Conversely, prolonged DHβE exposure upregulated ACh-induced currents, similar to the binding sites (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: DHβE did not occlude nicotine upregulation when the two ligands were co-incubated.
source: DHβE did not occlude nicotine upregulation when the two ligands were co-incubated, however, demonstrating that it has a different effect on functional upregulation than varenicline and lobeline.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding by DHβE was unchanged whether membranes were assayed or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment.
source: Like nicotine, we see no evidence of DHβE being trapped in binding assays; upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding was unchanged whether membranes were assayed (data not shown) or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment (Figure 3B, green columns in the right half of the graph).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Nicotine and DHβE are less likely than varenicline and lobeline to be trapped because they are less likely to be in their protonated form in an acidic compartment.
source: Based on this correlation between their physical properties and our current data, we propose that nicotine and DHβE are less likely than varenicline and lobeline to be trapped because they are less likely to be in their protonated form in an acidic compartment.
evidence: Inferred from pKa values in Table 1 and experimental data showing differential trapping.

claim: For exposures for 17–18 hr at concentrations up to 100 μM mecamylamine, there was no evidence of upregulation as assayed by 125I-epibatidine binding or by ACh-induced currents.
source: For exposures for 17–18 hr at concentrations up to 100 μM, there was no evidence of upregulation as assayed by 125I-epibatidine binding (Figure 3D) or by ACh-induced currents (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Acute application of mecamylamine (100 μM) inhibited ACh-induced currents.
source: Acute application of mecamylamine (100 μM) inhibited ACh-induced currents (data not shown) as previously observed (Wu et al., 2006), confirming that the drug had the expected pharmacological activity.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wu et al., 2006.

claim: There was no difference in mecamylamine binding when performed on membranes or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment.
source: Despite its high pKa value, we observed no evidence of mecamylamine being trapped because there was no difference in the binding when performed on membranes (data not shown) or if the pH gradient of acidic compartments was diminished with NH4Cl treatment (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Mecamylamine appears to readily cross the blood-brain barrier and cell membranes.
source: However, mecamylamine appears to readily cross the blood-brain barrier and cell membranes (Shytle et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shytle et al., 2002.

claim: Trapping requires high-affinity ligand binding to α4β2R located within acidic compartments.
source: A more likely possibility is that trapping also requires high-affinity ligand binding to α4β2R located within acidic compartments.
evidence: Inferred from mecamylamine's lack of trapping despite high pKa and its low affinity for α4β2R.

claim: The pKa value and affinity for epibatidine are both higher than those for varenicline and lobeline.
source: The pKa value and affinity for epibatidine are both higher than those for varenicline and lobeline (Table 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: Epibatidine (30 μM) did not promote upregulation of either 125I-epibatidine binding or ACh-induced currents in intact cells.
source: In intact cells, epibatidine (30 μM) did not promote upregulation of either 125I-epibatidine binding (Figure 3C left half, D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or ACh-induced currents (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and Figure 3F.

claim: Epibatidine reduced nicotine-induced upregulation in both binding and functional assays.
source: However, epibatidine reduced nicotine-induced upregulation in both assays (Figure 3C left half, D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C, 3D, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: With NH4Cl treatment, epibatidine upregulated 125I-epibatidine binding to 60% of the nicotine induced value.
source: With NH4Cl treatment, we observed upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding to 60% of the nicotine induced value and that nicotine upregulation was reduced by 40%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: With NH4Cl treatment, nicotine upregulation was reduced by 40% in the presence of epibatidine.
source: With NH4Cl treatment, we observed upregulation of 125I-epibatidine binding to 60% of the nicotine induced value and that nicotine upregulation was reduced by 40%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Epibatidine behaves in a qualitatively similar way as varenicline and lobeline with respect to upregulation and is subject to trapping in intracellular compartments.
source: Thus, epibatidine behaves in a qualitatively similar way as varenicline and lobeline with respect to upregulation and therefore is subject to trapping in intracellular compartments, consistent with the phenomenon arising from a combination of high binding affinity for the receptor and a very basic pKa.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing pH-dependent effects on epibatidine's actions.

claim: The association rate constant for 125I-epibatidine binding to α4β2Rs in living cells is 3.8 × 10^7 (M-sec)^−1.
source: However, the data are consistent with a single exponential process and an association rate constant of 3.8 × 107 (M-sec)−1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), similar to previous measurements using 3H-epibatidine on isolated membrane preparations containing α4β2Rs (Whiteaker et al., 1998; Gnädisch et al., 1999; Shafaee et al., 1999) and to intact cells (Whiteaker et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The single association rate is consistent with 125I-epibatidine binding with very similar rates to all cellular α4β2Rs.
source: The single association rate is consistent with 125I-epibatidine binding with very similar rates to all cellular α4β2Rs and indicates that the radioligand crosses cellular membranes rapidly enough that permeation does not significantly contribute to the binding rate (Figure 4E).
evidence: Inferred from single exponential association kinetics.

claim: The dissociation of 125I-epibatidine from α4β2R-expressing cells revealed a biphasic time course that was best fit as the sum of two exponential processes.
source: Second, analysis of the dissociation of 125I-epibatidine exiting the α4β2R-expressing cells revealed a biphasic time course that was best fit as the sum of two exponential processes (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The faster dissociating component of 125I-epibatidine (~40% of the total binding) had a rate constant of 1.5 × 10^−3 sec^−1 (τ = 11.4 min).
source: The faster dissociating component (τ = 11.4 min; 1.5 × 10−3 sec−1),~40% of the total binding, was similar to rates previously measured for unbinding of radio-labeled epibatidine from α4β2Rs in membrane fragments.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The slower dissociation component of 125I-epibatidine had a rate constant of 6.0 × 10^−6 sec^−1 (τ = 47 hr).
source: In contrast, the slower dissociation component (τ = 47 hr) had a rate constant of 6.0 × 10−6 sec−1 and therefore was >100 fold slower than previous measurements of 125I-epibatidine unbinding from α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The slow component of 125I-epibatidine dissociation was >100 fold slower than previous measurements of 125I-epibatidine unbinding from α4β2Rs.
source: In contrast, the slower dissociation component (τ = 47 hr) had a rate constant of 6.0 × 10−6 sec−1 and therefore was >100 fold slower than previous measurements of 125I-epibatidine unbinding from α4β2Rs.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and comparison to literature values.

claim: 0.10–0.20 pmol of 125I-epibatidine dissociated during the faster dissociation component, corresponding to a concentration of 0.2–0.4 nM free 125I-epibatidine in the assay volume.
source: We found that 0.10–0.20 pmol of 125I-epibatidine dissociated during the faster dissociation component in the assay shown in Figure 4A, which corresponds to a concentration of 0.2–0.4 nM free 125I-epibatidine in our 0.5 ml assay volume of the eppendorf tube used in these assays.
evidence: Calculated from experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Dissociation of 125I-epibatidine in the presence of 100 μM nicotine occurred with a much faster overall time course, such that the radioligand was released in less than a minute.
source: Dissociation of 125I-epibatidine in the presence of nicotine occurred with a much faster overall time course, such that the radioligand was released in less than a minute rather than being trapped for hours.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The rapid release of 125I-epibatidine in the presence of nicotine was followed by a slower time course of dissociation (τ = 24 min at 37°C) with a rate constant of 7.0 × 10^−4 sec^−1.
source: The rapid release of radioligand was followed by a slower time course of dissociation (τ = 24 min at 37°C), which is typical of rates (7.0 × 10−4 sec−1) previously measured for the dissociation of 3H-epibatidine from α4β2Rs and dissociation constants for affinity (KD = 18 pM) (Whiteaker et al., 1998; Gnädisch et al., 1999; Shafaee et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous studies.

claim: The addition of 100 nM nicotine only reduced the slow component of 125I-epibatidine dissociation by ~20%.
source: We tested this prediction in additional dissociation assays and instead found that the addition of 100 nM nicotine only reduced the slow component of dissociation by ~20% (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Higher concentrations of nicotine (100 μM – 10 mM) added into the dissociation assay act on both components of the trapping phenomenon: preventing 125I-epibatidine rebinding and reducing the pH gradient to neutralize acidic compartments.
source: Higher concentrations of nicotine (100 μM – 10 mM) added into the dissociation assay act on both components of the trapping phenomenon; that is, increasing nicotine concentrations not only prevented 125I-epibatidine rebinding but also reduced the pH gradient to neutralize acidic compartments, leading to deprotonation (and release) of 125I-epibatidine.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing concentration-dependent effects of nicotine on 125I-epibatidine dissociation (Figure 4C).

claim: The proportion of 125I-epibatidine dissociation contributed by the slower component decreased with increasing nicotine concentrations and saturated at a value of ~60% of the total 'bound' 125I-epibatidine for both the untreated and nicotine-treated cells.
source: This was evident in the fact that the proportion of 125I-epibatidine dissociation contributed by the slower component decreased with increasing nicotine concentrations and saturated at a value of ~60% of the total 'bound' 125I-epibatidine for both the untreated and nicotine-treated cells (Figure 4C), which is the entirety of the slowly dissociating component.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Chloroquine (150 μM) reduces the pH gradient of acidic compartment at similar concentrations to nicotine and has a similar effect on 125I-epibatidine binding.
source: Chloroquine (150 μM), a weak base with a molecular weight and pKa similar to that of nicotine, also reduces the pH gradient of acidic compartment at similar concentrations and has a similar effect on 125I-epibatidine binding (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: 125I-epibatidine binding to HEK cells lacking α4β2Rs was ~1% of that observed with nicotine upregulation.
source: 125I-epibatidine binding to these HEK cells was ~1% of that observed with nicotine upregulation and was equivalent to 'non-specific' binding obtained with 1 mM competing nicotine present during 125I-epibatidine binding and washing (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: No selective trapping of 125I-epibatidine occurs without α4β2R expression.
source: This finding demonstrates that no selective trapping of 125I-epibatidine occurs without α4β2R expression.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing minimal binding in cells lacking α4β2Rs (Figure 4D).

claim: Without high-affinity binding α4β2Rs, 125I-epibatidine concentrates within acidic vesicles but it rapidly exits the vesicles when its extracellular concentration falls.
source: Without high-affinity binding α4β2Rs, 125I-epibatidine concentrates within acidic vesicles but it rapidly exits the vesicles when its extracellular concentration falls.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing cells with and without α4β2Rs.

claim: High-affinity α4β2Rs in intracellular compartments trap 125I-epibatidine even when its extracellular concentration falls, whereas nicotine rapidly exits the acidic compartments.
source: High-affinity α4β2Rs in intracellular compartments trap 125I-epibatidine even when its extracellular concentration falls, whereas nicotine rapidly exits the acidic compartments.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing differential trapping of epibatidine versus nicotine.

claim: Nicotine upregulation did not change the relative contribution of either the fast or slow component of 125I-epibatidine dissociation.
source: Surprisingly, nicotine upregulation did not change the relative contribution of either the fast or slow component of radioligand dissociation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on dissociation kinetics.

claim: The fraction of 125I-epibatidine specifically bound to α4β2Rs remained at ~40% and the fraction trapped in intracellular compartments remained at ~60% with nicotine upregulation.
source: The fraction of 125I-epibatidine specifically bound to α4β2Rs remained at ~40% and the fraction of trapped in intracellular compartments and slowly released remained at ~60%.
evidence: Supported by experimental data on dissociation kinetics.

claim: Nicotine caused the fraction of trapped 125I-epibatidine to increase by 4–5-fold.
source: As displayed in Figure 4F, nicotine caused the fraction of trapped 125I-epibatidine to increase by 4–5-fold, the same fold increase observed for total (bound and trapped) 125I-epibatidine retained in the cells with nicotine exposure (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4D.

claim: The fraction of 125I-epibatidine specifically bound to the α4β2Rs increased 4–5-fold with nicotine exposure.
source: The fraction of 125I-epibatidine specifically bound to the α4β2Rs also increased 4–5-fold with nicotine exposure (data not shown).
evidence: Stated in the manuscript based on experimental data.

claim: SEP is a pH-sensitive variant of GFP that fluoresces at neutral pH but is quenched at pH values lower than 6.
source: SEP is a pH-sensitive variant of GFP that fluoresces at neutral pH but is quenched at pH values lower than 6.
evidence: Supported by established knowledge about super ecliptic pHluorin properties.

claim: Fluorescent α4SEP was found throughout the ER in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells and in cortical neurons, as indicated by co-localization with the ER marker, DsRed-ER.
source: When expressed in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells and in cortical neurons, florescent α4SEP was found throughout the ER, as indicated by co-localization with the ER marker, DsRed-ER (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,C), and on the cell surface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D) as previously observed (Richards et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,C and citation to Richards et al., 2011.

claim: Fluorescent α4SEP was found on the cell surface in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells and in cortical neurons.
source: When expressed in α4β2R-expressing HEK cells and in cortical neurons, florescent α4SEP was found throughout the ER, as indicated by co-localization with the ER marker, DsRed-ER (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,C), and on the cell surface (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D) as previously observed (Richards et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B,D and citation to Richards et al., 2011.

claim: NH4Cl treatment revealed an additional pool of the α4SEP subunits in what appeared to be small vesicles in HEK cells and cortical neurons.
source: As displayed in Figure 5A for the HEK cells and Figure 5B for the cortical neurons, NH4Cl treatment revealed an additional pool of the α4SEP subunits in what appeared to be small vesicles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5B.

claim: The α4SEP subunits in the acidic vesicles are likely mature, fully assembled α4β2Rs because receptor assembly occurs in the ER and entry into any acidic compartment occurs after exit from the ER.
source: It is likely that the α4SEP subunits in the acidic vesicles are mature, fully assembled α4β2Rs because receptor assembly occurs in the ER (Sallette et al., 2005) and entry into any acidic compartment occurs after exit from the ER.
evidence: Inferred from citation to Sallette et al., 2005 and knowledge of receptor trafficking.

claim: The number of α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles in the HEK cells and cortical neurons was greatly increased by the 17 hr nicotine exposure.
source: The number of α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles in the HEK cells and cortical neurons was greatly increased by the 17 hr nicotine exposure (Figure 5A,B,C) and paralleled the effect of nicotine on the number of high-affinity binding sites and the amount of 125I-epibatidine trapping (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B,C and Figure 4F.

claim: In the neurons, α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles were found in the processes, in what appeared to be both dendrites and axons, as well as in the somata.
source: In the neurons, α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles were found in the processes, in what appeared to be both dendrites and axons, as well as in the somata (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Nicotine upregulation occurs in part through an augmentation of the number of receptor-containing acidic vesicles.
source: These results demonstrate that nicotine upregulation occurs in part through an augmentation of the number of receptor-containing acidic vesicles.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing increased numbers of α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles with nicotine treatment.

claim: Varenicline exposure reduced nicotine upregulation of α4β2Rs independent of its pharmacological action as a partial agonist.
source: In this study, we find that the smoking cessation agent varenicline (Chantix) has significant effects on α4β2Rs independent of its pharmacological action as a partial agonist.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing effects that depend on intracellular pH and trapping, not just receptor activation.

claim: The effects of varenicline on upregulation required intact intracellular acidic vesicles containing α4β2Rs.
source: The effects of varenicline on upregulation required intact intracellular acidic vesicles containing α4β2Rs and were not observed if HEK cell or neuronal membranes were compromised.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential effects in live cells versus membrane preparations.

claim: The integrity of acidic compartments was lost in earlier studies that assayed binding using membrane fragments of brain tissue or autoradiography.
source: The integrity of acidic compartments was lost in earlier studies that assayed binding using membrane fragments of brain tissue or autoradiography (Marks et al., 1983; Schwartz and Kellar, 1983; Marks et al., 2015) accounting for the different actions of varenicline we observed in living cells.
evidence: Inferred from citations to previous studies and current experimental findings.

claim: Varenicline is selectively trapped as a weak base within intracellular acidic vesicles.
source: Based on our findings, it is evident that varenicline is selectively trapped as a weak base within intracellular acidic vesicles, and once trapped, it is slowly released from the vesicles and cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing pH-dependent effects and slow release kinetics.

claim: Once trapped, varenicline is slowly released from the vesicles and cells.
source: Based on our findings, it is evident that varenicline is selectively trapped as a weak base within intracellular acidic vesicles, and once trapped, it is slowly released from the vesicles and cells.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing slow release and transfer experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: The trapped varenicline competes with 125I-epibatidine binding to α4β2Rs within the acidic vesicles.
source: The trapped varenicline competes with 125I-epibatidine binding to α4β2Rs within the acidic vesicles while the slow release competes with 125I-epibatidine binding elsewhere in the cells and desensitizes cell-surface α4β2Rs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced 125I-epibatidine binding with varenicline treatment.

claim: The slow release of varenicline competes with 125I-epibatidine binding elsewhere in the cells and desensitizes cell-surface α4β2Rs.
source: The trapped varenicline competes with 125I-epibatidine binding to α4β2Rs within the acidic vesicles while the slow release competes with 125I-epibatidine binding elsewhere in the cells and desensitizes cell-surface α4β2Rs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing reduced ACh-evoked currents with varenicline treatment.

claim: Effects of varenicline on nicotine upregulation were observed at concentrations as low as 100 nM.
source: We observed effects of varenicline on nicotine upregulation at concentrations as low as 100 nM (Figure 1G), a concentration that is estimated to occur in human brain with prescribed varencline doses (Rollema et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and citation to Rollema et al., 2010.

claim: The approach used by Rollema et al. to estimate human brain varenicline concentrations likely significantly underestimated the levels of varenicline in brain.
source: As is evident from our study, this approach will not include varenicline trapping in acidic vesicles, which should serve as an additional high-capacity reservoir for varenicline in brain neurons, and is lost in the brain lysate preparation. Therefore, this study likely significantly underestimated the levels of varenicline in brain and the effects of trapping in acidic vesicles should be considered in future such estimates.
evidence: Inferred from current experimental findings showing trapping in acidic vesicles.

claim: The dose-dependence of all three weak base ligands that were trapped within intracellular acidic vesicles had an inverted U-shape where the peak of the curve occurs at ~1 μM concentration.
source: The dose-dependence of all three weak base ligands that were trapped within intracellular acidic vesicles had an inverted U-shape where the peak of the curve occurs at ~1 μM concentration.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The decline in the dose-dependence curve at concentrations greater than 1 μM is consistent with the weak base effect of the ligands at these concentrations increasing the pH within the vesicle lumen and thereby increasing the rate of release of the trapped ligand.
source: The decline in the dose-dependence curve at concentrations greater than 1 μM is consistent with the weak base effect of the ligands at these concentrations increasing the pH within the vesicle lumen and thereby increasing the rate of release of the trapped ligand.
evidence: Inferred from dose-response data and understanding of weak base chemistry.

claim: The decay time (t1/2) for the varenicline plasma concentration is 1 day.
source: The decay time (t1/2) for the varenicline plasma concentration is 1 day and the time to reach steady-state levels with repeated dosing is 4 days (Faessel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Faessel et al., 2010.

claim: The time to reach steady-state levels of varenicline with repeated dosing is 4 days.
source: The decay time (t1/2) for the varenicline plasma concentration is 1 day and the time to reach steady-state levels with repeated dosing is 4 days (Faessel et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Faessel et al., 2010.

claim: The decay time for the nicotine plasma concentration is 2 hr.
source: In contrast, the decay time for the nicotine plasma concentration to decay is 2 hr and the time to reach steady-state levels with repeated dosing is 2–3 hr (Benowitz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Benowitz et al., 2009.

claim: The time to reach steady-state levels of nicotine with repeated dosing is 2–3 hr.
source: In contrast, the decay time for the nicotine plasma concentration to decay is 2 hr and the time to reach steady-state levels with repeated dosing is 2–3 hr (Benowitz et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Benowitz et al., 2009.

claim: The differences in pharmacokinetic profiles between varenicline and nicotine are consistent with the slow exit rate measured for varenicline from acidic vesicles and the rapid exit of nicotine.
source: These differences are consistent with the slow exit rate we measured for varenicline from acidic vesicles and the rapid exit of nicotine.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on trapping and release kinetics and pharmacokinetic data from literature.

claim: Less than 10% of varenicline is metabolized over 2 hr.
source: The residence of a large amount of varenicline in α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles in neurons is likely also to contribute to the differences in the rate at which varenicline and nicotine are metabolized; nicotine is metabolized with the decay time of 2 hr, whereas less than 10% of varenicline is metabolized over this time.
evidence: Stated based on pharmacokinetic knowledge.

claim: The volume of distribution of varenicline is 5.9 L/Kg.
source: For varenicline, the volume of distribution (5.9 L/Kg; [Faessel et al., 2010]) is more than twice that for nicotine (2.6 L/Kg; [Benowitz et al., 2009]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Faessel et al., 2010.

claim: The volume of distribution of nicotine is 2.6 L/Kg.
source: For varenicline, the volume of distribution (5.9 L/Kg; [Faessel et al., 2010]) is more than twice that for nicotine (2.6 L/Kg; [Benowitz et al., 2009]).
evidence: Supported by citation to Benowitz et al., 2009.

claim: The volume of distribution of varenicline is more than twice that for nicotine.
source: For varenicline, the volume of distribution (5.9 L/Kg; [Faessel et al., 2010]) is more than twice that for nicotine (2.6 L/Kg; [Benowitz et al., 2009]).
evidence: Calculated from values cited from Faessel et al., 2010 and Benowitz et al., 2009.

claim: The difference in volume of distribution between varenicline and nicotine is consistent with and perhaps caused by trapping of varenicline within acidic compartments in cells and neurons and the absence of trapping for nicotine.
source: This difference again is consistent with and perhaps caused by trapping of varenicline within acidic compartments in cells and neurons and the absence of trapping for nicotine.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on trapping and pharmacokinetic data from literature.

claim: Varenicline trapping in acidic vesicles would create a high-capacity reservoir in neurons that express α4β2Rs.
source: Varenicline trapping in acidic vesicles would create a high-capacity reservoir in neurons that express α4β2Rs.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing trapping and slow release.

claim: Clinical efficacy of varenicline could result from sustained varenicline levels within neurons that leak out and desensitize α4β2Rs, and perhaps other nAChRs, and that activity counteracts the functional upregulation of nicotine exposure.
source: We predict that this phenomenon maintains relatively high and constant concentrations of varenicline, especially in contrast to nicotine levels that rise during the day and decline rapidly at night. Clinical efficacy could therefore result from sustained varenicline levels within neurons that leak out and desensitize α4β2Rs, and perhaps other nAChRs, and that activity counteracts the functional upregulation of nicotine exposure.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental findings about trapping and release.

claim: The presence of α4β2R provides the selectivity for long-lasting trapping of certain nicotinic weak base ligands in acidic vesicles.
source: As modeled in Figures 4E and 5D, the presence of α4β2R is what provides the selectivity for long-lasting trapping of certain nicotinic weak base ligands in acidic vesicles.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing requirement of α4β2Rs for trapping.

claim: Selective trapping requires a low enough pH in the vesicles to protonate weak base ligands and slow its exit.
source: Selective trapping also requires a low enough pH in the vesicles, to protonate weak base ligands and slows its exit.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data showing pH-dependent effects.

claim: Trapping only occurs when there are α4β2Rs in the vesicles and ligand pKa and affinity for α4β2Rs are sufficiently high.
source: Trapping only occurs when there are α4β2Rs in the vesicles and ligand pKa and affinity for α4β2Rs are sufficiently high.
evidence: Inferred from experimental data comparing different ligands with varying pKa and affinity values.

claim: Nicotine and DHβE fail to show the trapping phenomenon because they are not sufficiently protonated at low pH.
source: Nicotine and DHβE fail to show the trapping phenomenon for two reasons: nicotine and DHβE are not sufficiently protonated at low pH and DHβE also does not bind with high enough affinity to α4β2R.
evidence: Inferred from pKa values and experimental data showing lack of trapping.

claim: DHβE does not bind with high enough affinity to α4β2R to show trapping.
source: Nicotine and DHβE fail to show the trapping phenomenon for two reasons: nicotine and DHβE are not sufficiently protonated at low pH and DHβE also does not bind with high enough affinity to α4β2R.
evidence: Inferred from affinity values in Table 1 and experimental data showing lack of trapping.

claim: Epibatidine has a high pKa and affinity, and therefore accumulates and leaks back out over the course of days.
source: Epibatidine, on the other hand, has a high pKa and affinity, and therefore accumulates and leaks back out over the course of days, as was observed in our dissociation experiments (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by pKa and affinity values in Table 1 and experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Higher trapping levels of 125I-epibatidine with nicotine exposure were caused by a rise in the numbers of vesicles containing α4β2Rs.
source: Higher trapping levels were caused by a rise in the numbers of vesicles containing α4β2Rs as imaged using pH-sensitive, pHluorin-tagged α4 subunits in the α4β2R-expressing HEK cells and cultured neurons (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: It is not clear if the increases in α4β2R-containing acidic vesicles are caused by the formation of new vesicles or redistribution of α4β2Rs to preexisting vesicles.
source: However, it is not clear if the increases are caused by the formation of new vesicles or redistribution of α4β2Rs to preexisting vesicles.
evidence: Acknowledged limitation of current experimental data.

claim: Surface α4β2R degradation through late endosomes and lysosomes is not increased by nicotine upregulation.
source: In this study, we did not distinguish among these possibilities, but our previous findings and those of others (Vallejo et al., 2005; Darsow et al., 2005) indicate that surface α4β2R degradation through late endosomes and lysosomes is not increased by nicotine upregulation; therefore, the acidic vesicles are unlikely to be either of these organelles.
evidence: Supported by citations to Vallejo et al., 2005 and Darsow et al., 2005.

claim: The acidic vesicles containing α4β2Rs are unlikely to be late endosomes or lysosomes.
source: In this study, we did not distinguish among these possibilities, but our previous findings and those of others (Vallejo et al., 2005; Darsow et al., 2005) indicate that surface α4β2R degradation through late endosomes and lysosomes is not increased by nicotine upregulation; therefore, the acidic vesicles are unlikely to be either of these organelles.
evidence: Inferred from citations to Vallejo et al., 2005 and Darsow et al., 2005.

claim: If the smoking cessation activity of varenicline is caused by its trapping in intracellular acidic vesicles, then the findings should help guide the design of more effective smoking cessation drugs.
source: If the smoking cessation activity of varenicline is indeed caused by its trapping in intracellular acidic vesicles, then our findings should help guide the design of more effective smoking cessation drugs.
evidence: Speculative inference based on experimental findings.

claim: The selective and regulated trapping observed for varenicline may occur for weak base ligands that bind with high-affinity to other types of receptors, ion channels or transporters.
source: The selective and regulated trapping we observe for varenicline also may occur for weak base ligands that bind with high-affinity to other types of receptors, ion channels or transporters.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from current findings.

claim: Most drugs of abuse are weak base ligands that bind with varying affinities to a variety of different membrane proteins.
source: Most drugs of abuse are weak base ligands that bind with varying affinities to a variety of different membrane proteins (Sulzer, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sulzer, 2011.

claim: Amphetamines are weak bases with pKa values in the range of 8 to 10 that can concentrate in acidic vesicles and affect the catecholamine quantum size in synaptic vesicles and chromaffin granules.
source: In particular, amphetamines are weak bases with pKa values in the range of 8 to 10 that can concentrate in acidic vesicles and affect the catecholamine quantum size in synaptic vesicles and chromaffin granules (Sulzer et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sulzer et al., 2005.

claim: Certain antipsychotic drugs are weak bases that accumulate in and are released from synaptic vesicles.
source: Certain antipsychotic drugs are weak bases that accumulate in and are released from synaptic vesicles (Tischbirek et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tischbirek et al., 2012.

claim: Weak bases that bind with high-affinity to the binding sites where other drugs of abuse bind could serve as cessation agents similar to varenicline.
source: Weak bases that bind with high-affinity to the binding sites where other drugs of abuse bind could serve as cessation agents similar to varenicline.
evidence: Speculative extrapolation from current findings about varenicline.
